newsitem.title: GERMANY: German SPD wants Bonn report on Elf funds charge.
newsitem.headline: German SPD wants Bonn report on Elf funds charge.

text.p: Opposition Social Democrats (SPD) demanded on Wednesday the Bonn government report to parliament on the circumstances surrounding the purchase of an east German petrochemical plant by the French oil company Elf-Aquitaine.

Peter Struck, SPD whip in parliament, said he saw no basis for accusations in the French press that Elf had paid 13.5 million marks ($7.8 million) in bribes to win the contract for the Leuna plant and Minol petrol station network.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democratic Union (CDU), the purported recipient of the funds, has flatly denied the story in the Le Parisien daily that it had taken the bribes. Elf has had no comment either in Germany or in Paris.
And in Paris the public prosecutor's office said on Wednesday there was no evidence to suggest Kohl's CDU had received covert funds from a businessman under judicial investigation in France.

"Indications published recently referring to the financing of a foreign political party are not based on any evidence in the investigation being conducted by judge Eva Joly," the spokesman for the prosecutor's office told Reuters.

Joly received authorisation from the prosecutor's office on Monday to widen an investigation into alleged financial irregularities at Elf while Loik Le Floch-Prigent was chairman from 1988 to 1993 to cover suspect payments to Germany.

In Bonn SPD whip Struck noted that Kohl had used his political influence to ensure that a French investor made the five billion mark purchase in 1992, one of the last megadeals by the Treuhand holding company privatising former communist industry.
This was seen at the time as another sign of Germany's close postwar ties with its one-time enemy France.
"Should it turn out that extraneous consideration played a role in granting the contract to Elf-Aquitaine, then there will certainly be considerable consequences," he told Berlin's InfoRadio station.
The SPD had no plan to call for a parliamentary inquiry, he said, but added: "It could come if the report by (Finance Minister Theo) Waigel indicates things were not completely correct."
CDU secretary general Peter Hintze flatly denied the bribery charge on Tuesday, saying: "The CDU has never received funds from France, either directly or indirectly.
"This is an especially malicious invention and a nauseating charge and I find it especially bad that this is linked to a bid to harm the good relations between Germany and France."

The newspaper Le Parisien said on Tuesday that Elf had paid a 13.5 million mark ($7.8 million) commission to a Liechtenstein-based company -- Noblepac -- in connection with its purchase of the Leuna and Minol firms.

Le Parisien said Noblepac transferred the funds further, mainly to Germany, including to the CDU via an unnamed Bavarian intermediary, and that a magistrate wanted to trace the recipients of the money.
Noblepac is owned by Andre Guelfi, an intermediary who is already under judicial investigation in the case.

The Elf case began as an investigation of alleged financial irregularities when Loik Le Floch-Prigent was chairman in 1988-93. It has since widened to cover Elf's operations and commission payments abroad, including dealings in Gabon and Venezuela.
